Crabeater seals exhibit a tightly constrained reproductive schedule that reflects the extreme seasonality of the Antarctic pack ice ecosystem. Gestation, encompassing the period from fertilization to parturition, has been documented to last for 259 days [tg = 259 days] at the core body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C] that is characteristic of this phocid species. This duration aligns closely with the annual cycle of sea ice advance and retreat, ensuring that pups are born during the austral spring when prey availability is maximal and ice conditions are optimal for neonatal survival. Female crabeater seals typically give birth to a single pup per litter [N_R_i = single pup per litter], and breeding occurs approximately once every two years [F_R_i = approximately once every two years], a pattern that yields a maximum reproductive rate of one pup every two years. This relatively slow reproductive tempo is consistent with the energy demands of lactation in a high-latitude marine predator. The extended gestation interval likely reflects the metabolic constraints imposed by a foraging ecology centered on Antarctic krill, which undergoes pronounced seasonal fluctuations in abundance and caloric density.

Neonatal crabeater seals emerge onto the pack ice at a remarkably modest body mass compared to the adult form, with newborns weighing approximately 36,000 grams [Wwb = approximately 36,000 grams] at birth. This substantial absolute mass, however, belies the fact that pups are relatively lean compared to the lipid-rich neonates of some other phocid species, reflecting the crabeater seal's reliance on a relatively low-energy, high-protein krill-based milk rather than a fat-rich diet. Maternal investment during the brief nursing period is intense, as the pup must nearly double its birth weight before facing the challenges of independent foraging. The period from birth to nutritional independence is remarkably compressed, with weaning occurring at just 28 days after parturition [tx = 28 days after parturition] when measured at maternal body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. This abbreviated lactation interval is among the shortest documented for any true seal of comparable body size and represents an adaptive response to the precarious and ephemeral nature of the pack ice platform, which begins to break up and disperse shortly after the pupping season concludes.

Adult body size in crabeater seals exhibits pronounced sexual dimorphism, with females typically attaining a larger ultimate wet weight than males. Data from long-term field studies in the Weddell Sea and the Antarctic Peninsula indicate that the maximum recorded adult body mass for females is approximately 215,000 grams [Wwi = approximately 215,000 grams], making them among the largest of the Antarctic pack ice seals relative to their moderate cranial dimensions. Males, by contrast, tend to cap their growth at a somewhat lower asymptotic mass of around 200,000 grams [Wwi = around 200,000 grams], a difference that is thought to reflect divergent reproductive strategies: females prioritize body size to buffer the energetic costs of gestation and lactation, whereas males allocate resources toward the development of secondary sexual characteristics and the maintenance of breeding territories. This size disparity is also reflected in divergent life history trajectories, as the two sexes reach sexual maturity at different ages when assessed at the standard mammalian body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C]. Female crabeater seals attain puberty at 4 years after birth [tp = 4 years after birth], while males require a longer developmental period, reaching sexual maturity at 4.5 years after birth [tp = 4.5 years after birth] at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C] at a temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C].

Longevity records for crabeater seals, derived from tag-recapture studies and analysis of growth layers in tooth cementum, indicate that the species is relatively long-lived among Antarctic phocids. The maximum lifespan has been estimated at 39 years [am = 39 years] when assessed at the standard body temperature of 37 °C [T = 37 °C], a value that places the crabeater seal among the more enduring members of the Lobodontini tribe. This extended lifespan is consistent with a life history strategy that prioritizes adult survival over high reproductive output, a pattern common among marine mammals inhabiting unpredictable and resource-limited polar environments. The combination of a long lifespan, a relatively low annual reproductive rate of one pup per litter every two years, and delayed sexual maturation suggests that crabeater seals exhibit a slow-paced life history more akin to baleen whales than to many other pinniped lineages. However, this longevity also exposes individuals to the cumulative effects of anthropogenic stressors, including changing sea ice dynamics and potential perturbations to krill population structure induced by climate change and industrial fishing.

The crabeater seal's life history can be contextualized within a broader comparative framework of mammalian reproductive strategies. The combination of a 259-day gestation period spanning more than eight months, a single precocial pup weighing 36,000 grams at birth, and a condensed 28-day weaning interval represents a distinctive adaptive syndrome tailored to the ephemeral pack ice habitat. This syndrome is further characterized by the divergence in pubertal timing between sexes, with females maturing at 4 years after birth and males at 4.5 years after birth, a delay that likely reflects the competitive demands of male-male agonistic interactions during the breeding season. The ultimate adult masses of roughly 215,000 grams for females and 200,000 grams for males represent the culmination of a growth trajectory that extends over several years and is tightly coupled to krill availability. Longevity of up to 39 years enables multiple reproductive bouts across a female's lifetime, despite the intrinsically low per-event output of a single pup every two years. This suite of traits positions the crabeater seal as a classic K-selected strategist within the Antarctic marine ecosystem.
